subject: 🙏 Economic gratitude
body_html:
Plus: Consumer confidence surge | Tuesday, November 24, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Nov 24, 2026

With a flurry of economic data due out tomorrow, we're bringing you our annual Thanksgiving tradition a day early: five economic trends that make us thankful. 🦃

Situational awareness: Consumer confidence surged this month to its highest level since early last year, the Conference Board said. The research group attributed the 12.4% gain in its index to the resolution of the midterm elections and easing gasoline prices.

  • Separately, Bloomberg reports that the Federal Reserve's inspector general is investigating whether vice chair for supervision Michelle Bowman violated communication rules by appearing at a bank-sponsored event during the central bank's monetary policy blackout period.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 1,135 words, a 4.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Five reasons for economic gratitude
 

Photo illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios. Photo: Library of Congress
 

Not all the economic surprises of 2026 have been unpleasant. Some developments offer good reason to be optimistic about the years ahead.

  • Here are five we are grateful for ahead of Thanksgiving.

1. The productivity revival

After years of lackluster productivity growth, the U.S. economy is getting better at producing more with the same amount of labor. Stronger productivity growth creates room for businesses to raise wages without raising prices, and for the economy to grow faster without fueling inflation.

  • The productivity numbers are already encouraging, even before the transformative economic benefits promised by AI are clearly visible in the data.
  • Labor productivity has grown at a 2.5% annual pace since early 2023, according to San Francisco Fed research. That's well above the 1.5% pace that prevailed from 2005 to 2022, though short of the 3.3% recorded during the technology boom of the late 1990s and early 2000s.
  • That has obviously come with some existential angst about the future of human labor in the era of AI. But we spent too much time handwringing about the weak productivity gains of the 2010s — and related sluggish growth in incomes — not to view this shift with optimism.

2. The entrepreneurship boom

Americans are applying to start new businesses at the fastest pace on record, with more than 5 million applications filed in the first 10 months of this year, according to Census Bureau data.

  • There are early clues that AI may be fueling a new wave of entrepreneurship by making it easier to launch and run a business without employees.

By the numbers: Businesses less likely to hire employees accounted for 86% of the increase in new business applications in the first 10 months of the year, compared with the same period in 2025 — a sign of a burgeoning "solopreneur" economy, though some of these categorized businesses may eventually hire workers.

  • The boom is also evident in data from payments company Stripe. The number of new businesses launching on its platform each week has roughly doubled from a year ago, CEO Patrick Collison said last week at a Fed conference — a rate of growth without precedent in Stripe's 15-year history.

3. Low, low layoffs

This time a year ago, there was deep angst over the outlook for the labor market, as companies looked to an AI-powered future and the unemployment rate edged up.

  • But not only has the headline unemployment rate held steady at low levels this year, but the rate at which companies are laying people off is near all-time lows.

State of play: The rate at which employers laid off or discharged workers was 1% in September, only a tick above the 0.9% low in a data series that dates to 2001.

  • That rate averaged 1.2% in 2019, which was then viewed as a healthy labor market.
  • Weekly data on unemployment insurance claims tell the same story. The four-week moving average of initial claims has been below 200,000 in recent weeks.
  • Those are the lowest levels on record in a data series dating to 1967 — a time when the labor force was much smaller.

Zoom out: Getting a job is challenging in some sectors, as hiring rates are relatively low, especially in white-collar professions. But those who have a job have been able to hold onto it this year at historically high rates.

2. Two more for the road ...
 
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics and Energy Information Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

4. People can handle high gas prices better

There's no doubt that gasoline prices have risen a lot since the Iran war began in March. But households are better positioned to handle those costs than they were in the past.

Zoom in: The average nationwide price of a gallon of gasoline was $3.64 last week, per the Energy Information Administration — up from $2.94 in late February.

  • But $4 gasoline is a considerably smaller burden relative to wages and overall spending than it was in past energy shocks.

We like to look at gasoline prices in terms of how long a typical laborer — someone making the average hourly earnings for production and nonsupervisory workers — would have to work to afford a gallon.

  • In October, that figure was just shy of 8 minutes. That was nearly 11 minutes during the onset of the Ukraine war in 2022.
  • It was at or above 10 minutes for most of the period from early 2011 to the fall of 2014, as well as from the spring of 2007 to the fall of 2008.

Of note: Energy is also a smaller share of household spending than it once was, reflecting greater energy efficiency of modern cars and household appliances.

  • In September, gasoline and other energy goods were 2.4% of total personal consumption expenditures. Twenty years ago, that figure was 3.5%.

5. America's financial dominance

The U.S. remains at the center of the global financial system, giving American companies an extraordinary ability to raise money to finance growth and innovation.

  • Set aside the day-to-day swings in Anthropic's stock price: The 5-year-old company pulled off the largest IPO in history last week, raising more than $90 billion for its own coffers before fees.
  • The two largest IPOs in world history took place in the U.S. this year: SpaceX and Anthropic.

Two episodes this year suggest investors still turn to traditional U.S. safe-haven assets in times of turmoil.

  • The dollar rallied following the outbreak of the Iran war, and it's the strongest since before President Trump's "liberation day" tariffs in April 2025.
  • Long-term Treasury yields fell during last week's stock market sell-off in a classic flight to safety, despite stubborn inflation and the prospect of further Fed rate hikes.

America's AI investment boom is helping sustain its growth advantage. The International Monetary Fund, for instance, projects the U.S. economy will grow 2.3% next year — faster than any other G7 nation.

The bottom line: The U.S. economy has plenty of problems, and nobody would claim that all is perfect. But there are striking areas of resilience and strength that we can be grateful for this Thanksgiving.
